core.text: Every Latin noun changes its ending to show its job in the sentence. Naming who or what the sentence is about — the doer, or the thing being described — is the job of **the nominative (the plain naming form)**, *cāsus nōminātīvus*. It is the form the dictionary gives: *puella* (girl), *servus* (slave), *oppidum* (town). Latin does not rely on word order: the subject may come first, last or in the middle, and the ending marks it.
The subject is the person or thing the sentence is about, usually before the verb: *the girl* sings. A word after *is* that renames the subject (*Julia is a girl*) belongs with it.
The subject, and any word that renames it after *est* / *sunt* (is / are), stands in the nominative: singular -a, -us, -um; plural -ae, -ī, -a.

invented.en: The girl sings, the boy laughs.
The slaves are working in the garden.

core.text: *Mārcus Iūliam pulsat* and *Iūlia Mārcum pulsat* use the same two names, but the endings, not the order, say who hits whom. The doer keeps the naming form (*Mārcus*, *Iūlia*); the one it is done to takes -m, the accusative (the object form). A word ending in -m is not the subject.

more.text: The learner's notes sort nouns by their first form: a-nouns (*ūva*, grape), us-nouns (*caseus*, cheese) and um-nouns (*pōculum*, cup); nouns in -r or -er (*vir*, man; *culter*, knife; *puer*, boy) count as us-nouns with a missing -us. Some change their stem before any ending is added (*culter, cultr-ī*; *carō, carn-is*), which is why a second form is learned with the word.

Plurals: -a becomes -ae, -us becomes -ī, -um becomes -a. That neuter plural -a looks like a feminine singular: *oppida* is 'towns', never 'a town'. Nouns of the other declensions (*pānis*, *pānēs*) follow later.

After *est* / *sunt* the word that describes or renames the subject is also nominative (*Nīlus fluvius est*; *Sicilia īnsula magna est*): both halves of an 'A is B' sentence wear the same ending. Ørberg's cap. I sets out singulāris / plūrālis; A&G §339 gives the nominative as the case of the subject and §283 the predicate nominative.
